passage: You want to know why I was such a wall on the museum trip, Sunaina? Okay. I'm Zainab, and I'd decided before the bus even came that nobody in 10C liked me. New school, new city, everyone already in pairs. So I got on first, took the window, put my earphones in with nothing playing, and stared at the flyover like it was fascinating. When you asked if the seat was free, I said "whatever" without looking up. You sat somewhere else. At the museum I trailed at the back and yawned, loudly, to show I didn't care. By lunch nobody was even trying. And I thought, see? Told you. It took me till March, when you said you'd all thought I hated you, to realise I'd written the whole story myself and then acted it out.

qa.q: What did Zainab say when Sunaina asked if the seat was free?
qa.a: "Whatever", without looking up.

qa.q: What did Zainab believe before the bus came, and how did that belief shape the day?
qa.a: Zainab was sure nobody in 10C liked the new student, so the silent earphones, the yawns and the one-word answer all came from expecting rejection.

qa.q: Where was the turning point on the bus, and what could Zainab have done instead?
qa.a: When Sunaina asked about the seat, Zainab could have taken the earphones out and said "yes, sit", a small risk that might have changed the whole trip.

qa.q: How did Zainab look to the rest of 10C that day?
qa.a: To them Zainab seemed bored and unfriendly, so they stopped trying, which is why they later said they thought Zainab hated them.

grounding: A new student expects classmates to dislike them, acts bored and distant on a trip, and the class's withdrawal seems to prove the belief.

passage: I'm Farida, and I've played on the colony basketball team for two years. Rehana joined in July. From day one she sat at the far end of the bench, scrolling, and when we did the circle chant before games she stood a step outside it with her arms folded. If someone passed her the ball in warm-ups, she passed it straight back without a word. After a couple of weeks people stopped passing to her. Stopped asking if she wanted chai after practice, too. Last Sunday I heard her tell her brother at the gate, "Told you. They don't want me there." I nearly laughed, because we'd all decided she didn't want us. I can't know what's going on in her head. But on Tuesday I'm going to sit at the far end of the bench and see what happens.

qa.q: Where did Rehana sit from day one?
qa.a: At the far end of the bench, scrolling.

qa.q: What does Rehana's "Told you. They don't want me there" suggest she expected all along?
qa.a: It suggests she expected rejection from the start and took the team's pulling back as proof, without seeing that her own distance had helped cause it.

qa.q: What is Farida's plan for Tuesday, and why might it break the loop?
qa.a: Farida plans to sit at Rehana's end of the bench; one friendly move could give Rehana different evidence from the story she expected.

qa.q: How had the team read Rehana's folded arms and silence?
qa.a: The team decided Rehana didn't want them, so they stopped passing and inviting, each side reading the other as the one who wasn't interested.

grounding: A teammate watches a new player who seems to expect rejection hold herself apart, so the others pull back, which she takes as proof.

passage: Thomas, you've just got your first two apprentices, so let old Wasim tell you something. In 1989, at the press, I had two nineteen-year-olds, Bashir and Anthony. Bashir was loud and quick, so I gave him the colour machine, the hard one. Anthony was quiet, so I gave him sweeping and bundling. I told myself I was being sensible. A year later Bashir could run any job in the building. He'd asked me a hundred questions and I'd answered every one. Anthony was still bundling. I'd barely spoken to him in months, except to say "faster". Then one night I found him fixing a jammed roller that had beaten me. He'd been watching from the corner all year. I felt sick. He hadn't stood still; I had kept him still. Give both of yours the hard machine. See who they become.

qa.q: What work did Wasim give Anthony?
qa.a: Sweeping and bundling.

qa.q: Why did Wasim feel sick on finding Anthony fixing the jammed roller?
qa.a: Wasim realised Anthony had real skill all along, and that Wasim's low expectations, not Anthony's ability, had kept Anthony still.

qa.q: What advice does Wasim give Thomas, and what would it change?
qa.a: Give both apprentices the hard machine, so each gets the same attention, answers and feedback instead of being sorted early.

qa.q: What might that year have been like for Anthony?
qa.a: Anthony heard little but "faster" and learnt quietly from the corner, probably feeling overlooked while still wanting to learn.

grounding: An elder foreman recalls noticing that the apprentice given hard work and attention grew fast, while the one kept on simple tasks was held back.

passage: The banquet was for four hundred, two cooks were down with fever, and the gas pressure kept dropping. Sudha, running the hotel kitchen, had no choice. "Jomon, take the gravy station." Jomon, nineteen, looked up from the mountain of onions he had been chopping for five months. "Me, chef?" "You." Across the kitchen, Reshma, whom Sudha had trained on sauces since her first day, was already plating starters without being told. Sudha kept half an eye on Jomon. He tasted, adjusted the salt, asked one sharp question about the cream, and burnt nothing. At midnight, scrubbing down, Sudha thought about Reshma's quick rise. Every week she had corrected Reshma's sauces, praised them, pushed her. To Jomon she had said almost nothing but "finer". Maybe that was the whole difference. Next morning she put Jomon's name on the sauce rota.

qa.q: How long had Jomon been chopping onions?
qa.a: For five months.

qa.q: What was Sudha thinking about while scrubbing down at midnight?
qa.a: She was realising that her weekly feedback and pushing had helped Reshma rise, while her near-silence toward Jomon may have kept him stuck.

qa.q: What did Sudha choose to do the next morning, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She put Jomon on the sauce rota, giving him the same chance, attention and feedback that had helped Reshma grow.

qa.q: What might "Me, chef?" reveal about how Jomon had come to see himself?
qa.a: It suggests five months of onions had taught him not to expect real responsibility, so being trusted came as a surprise.

grounding: A head cook notices that the junior she coached on hard tasks rose quickly, while the one she kept on simple work stalled until trusted in a crisis.

subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]
passage:
Monday. Darshan got the call: interview on Thursday, junior analyst. "They'll grill me on statistics and I'll blank," he told Kishore over dinner. Kishore offered to run practice questions with him. "Pointless. Either I know it or I don't." He watched a cricket match instead.
Thursday. In the waiting room his palms were wet. When the panel asked about regression, he heard himself say, "Sorry, I'm not good at this part," before he'd even tried. He stumbled through the case study he had never looked at, avoiding their eyes.
Saturday. The rejection email came. "See?" he told Kishore, almost relieved. "Knew it." Kishore didn't argue. He only asked, "How many practice questions did you do?" Darshan opened his mouth, then shut it.

qa.q: What did Darshan do instead of practice questions?
qa.a: He watched a cricket match.

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel almost relieved on Saturday?
qa.a: The rejection matched his prediction, so it felt like proof he had been right rather than something he had helped cause.

qa.q: Where was the real turning point, and what could Darshan have chosen then?
qa.a: On Monday, when Kishore offered practice questions; saying yes, even for an hour on regression, might have changed Thursday.

qa.q: Why might Kishore ask a question instead of arguing?
qa.a: Kishore likely saw that the fear had shaped the preparation, and a question lets Darshan notice it himself instead of feeling lectured.

grounding: A young adult sure an interview will go badly skips preparation, freezes in the room, and takes the rejection as proof he was right.

subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]
passage: Kamal, you keep saying the interview will be a disaster. Sit down; your Ishita Bua has a confession. In 1998 I was twenty-four and got a call for an announcer's job at the radio station. I was certain they wanted someone polished, someone from the city. So I didn't practise reading aloud even once. Why bother? The night before, I barely slept, sure of the ending. In the booth my voice shook so badly I lost my place twice. They were kind. They didn't take me. And I went home and told everyone, "I told you so," as if I'd won something. Two years later the same station called me again. That time I read the news aloud to your grandfather every night for a month. I got it. Same girl, same voice. The only thing that changed was what I did with the fear.

qa.q: What job was Ishita called for in 1998?
qa.a: An announcer's job at the radio station.

qa.q: Why did Ishita say "I told you so" after the rejection, as if something had been won?
qa.a: Being right about the failure felt safer than admitting that skipping practice had helped cause it; the prediction came true, so it felt like proof.

qa.q: What did Ishita do differently the second time, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Ishita read the news aloud every night for a month, preparing instead of predicting, which gave a steadier voice in the booth.

qa.q: How might Kamal hear "Same girl, same voice"?
qa.a: Kamal may realise the difference was preparation, not talent, so the coming interview is not already decided.

grounding: An elder recalls being sure an interview would fail, skipping practice, shaking in the booth and taking the rejection as proof, before preparing properly years later.

passage: On his first day as team lead at the logistics office in Kolkata, Suraj noticed the old thought arrive: they'll resent me, I'm younger than half of them. He knew that voice. It usually sent him to hide in his cabin. So he did the opposite, in small ways. At lunch he pulled a chair up to the team's table and asked about the new routing system first. He prepared a one-page note for each person's one-on-one. When Mrs Ghosh laughed at his joke about the printer, he wrote it down that night: evidence, not proof, but evidence. The others had warned him about Varun. "Careless. Check everything he does." Suraj gave Varun the Durgapur routes anyway, with a clear deadline and a check-in on Wednesday. On Wednesday Varun came in with the plan done and two good questions. Suraj wrote that down too.

qa.q: What did Suraj prepare for each person's one-on-one?
qa.a: A one-page note.

qa.q: What was Suraj worried about on the first day as team lead?
qa.a: He worried the team would resent him for being younger than half of them, a fear that had made him hide in the past.

qa.q: Which small choices helped Suraj act against the old forecast?
qa.a: Sitting at the team's table and speaking first, preparing for each one-on-one, and writing down small signs of warmth as evidence rather than proof.

qa.q: How might Varun have experienced being given the routes despite his reputation?
qa.a: Varun was trusted with a clear deadline and a check-in instead of being watched as careless, which may be why he came in prepared with questions.

grounding: A young team lead notices a forecast of being resented, acts against it in small ways, treats the results as new evidence and holds a junior to high but fair expectations.

passage:
"Vikas, you've been standing by the gate for ten minutes."
"I know, Darshan. I'm doing that thing. Telling myself they'll all have big jobs and look at me like the one who stayed back."
"And?"
"And last time I believed it, I stood in a corner, left early, and decided nobody cared. Which proved it."
"So what now?"
"Now I walk in and say hello first. To three people. That's the rule."
"Three?"
"Three. Then I decide what's true."
Forty minutes later, by the snacks table:
"Well?"
"Rukhsana asked about my bakery. Twice. Arun wants a cake for his daughter's birthday."
"And the third?"
"Didn't remember me at all." Vikas grinned. "That's fine. Two out of three is new evidence."

qa.q: How many people did Vikas decide to greet first?
qa.a: Three people.

qa.q: What was Vikas afraid of at the gate?
qa.a: Vikas was afraid the old friends would all have big jobs and look down on the one who stayed back.

qa.q: What choice broke the loop from last time?
qa.a: Instead of standing in a corner and leaving early, Vikas walked in and said hello first to three people, then judged by what actually happened.

qa.q: What would change if Vikas had counted only the person who forgot?
qa.a: Vikas would have gone home with the old story confirmed; treating the two warm replies as new evidence kept the result honest 🙂

grounding: A person notices a forecast of being looked down on at a reunion, acts against it by greeting people first, and treats what happens as new evidence.

passage: I'm Divyansh. Last month Harish and I both failed the geography test. We got 8 out of 25 each. On the bus I tore mine into little bits and said, "I'm stupid. I'll always be stupid at maps." Harish just looked at his paper. "I didn't learn the rivers chapter. That's all the questions." Then he folded it into his bag. That week he learnt the rivers with his sister. I didn't open the book, because what was the point? In the next test Harish got 19. I got 9. Now, when I'm stuck, I try saying "I didn't learn it yet." It feels less heavy.

qa.q: What did Harish say about the rivers chapter?
qa.a: "I didn't learn the rivers chapter. That's all the questions."

qa.q: Why did Divyansh tear the test into little bits on the bus?
qa.a: Divyansh felt ashamed and hopeless, sure of being "stupid at maps" forever, so the paper felt like proof.

qa.q: Which way of explaining the bad mark worked better, and why?
qa.a: Harish's, because blaming one unlearnt chapter pointed to something fixable, so he studied the rivers and got 19 next time.

qa.q: What would change if Divyansh had explained the mark the way Harish did?
qa.a: Divyansh might have opened the book that week instead of giving up, and the next mark could have looked more like 19 than 9.

grounding: Two children fail the same test; one decides they are stupid and stops trying, while the other blames an unlearnt chapter and studies it.

passage:
Tuition teacher's note, Class 6 batch, Friday.
Today I returned the fractions test. Vasudha and Sachin both scored 6 out of 20. Sachin frowned and said, "I didn't do the word problems at home. I'll do them this weekend." Vasudha pushed her paper away. "I'm just dumb at maths. I always will be." She would not pick up her pencil for the rest of the hour. After class I sat with her and asked her to circle every mistake. All of them were in the word problems; the sums she had practised were right. I asked, "So which is it, dumb at maths, or haven't practised these yet?" She was quiet a while, then said, "Haven't practised these." I have given her five word problems for Monday and will check them with her first.

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Sachin each score?
qa.a: 6 out of 20.

qa.q: Why wouldn't Vasudha pick up her pencil for the rest of the hour?
qa.a: She explained the bad mark as permanent, being "just dumb at maths", so trying again felt pointless to her.

qa.q: Why did asking Vasudha to circle every mistake help?
qa.a: It showed every mistake was in the word problems, turning "dumb at maths" into a specific gap she could practise.

qa.q: How might Sachin's weekend differ from Vasudha's, given how each explained the mark?
qa.a: Sachin saw a temporary cause and had a clear task for the weekend; Vasudha, before the teacher's help, had only a heavy belief about herself.

grounding: Two children fail the same test; one calls it a permanent flaw and stops, the other blames missing practice and plans to fix it.

passage: In the school auditorium in Chandigarh, the Class 10 play rehearsal stopped dead. Baljeet had forgotten the second line of the big speech, again. Ma'am said, "Take it from the top." Baljeet shook his head, face hot. On the bench outside afterwards he told Payal, "I'm quitting. And the debate team. I mess up everything I touch." "It's one line," Payal said. "It's not one line. It's me. It's always been me." He said it calmly, like reading out a weather report. "I'm not being dramatic. I'm just being realistic." Payal remembered him saying the same in Class 8 about football, and then chess. Each time he had quit within a week. "Realistic would be: you learnt that whole speech in four days," she said. Baljeet shrugged and walked to the bus stop, the script still in his hand.

qa.q: Which two things did Baljeet say he was quitting?
qa.a: The play and the debate team.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet believe he was being realistic?
qa.a: He saw one forgotten line as proof of a permanent flaw that spoils everything, so the gloomy view felt like plain fact to him.

qa.q: At this turning point, what could Baljeet try instead of quitting?
qa.a: He could treat it as one line that needs practice, not a verdict on himself, and run the speech a few more times before deciding anything.

qa.q: How does Payal see Baljeet's 'realism'?
qa.a: Payal sees a pattern of football, chess and now the play, each dropped within a week, and thinks the real facts, like learning the speech in four days, point the other way.

grounding: A teenager treats one forgotten line as proof he ruins everything, calls it realism, and moves to give up quickly.

passage:
"Navneet, coach wants us back for extra practice on Friday."
"I'm not coming, Thomas. I'm done with football."
"Because of one penalty?"
"Because I'm the kind of person who misses penalties. And fails chemistry. And forgot Mum's birthday. It's everything."
"You forgot her birthday?"
"Last year. See? It's a pattern."
"Okay, but you scored twice in the semi."
"Luck."
"So the miss is you, and the goals are luck?"
"That's just how it works for me."
"That's a weird rule."
"It's not a rule. It's the truth. I'm being honest."
"Come Friday anyway. Take five penalties. If you miss all five, fine, I'll stop asking."
"...I'll think about it."

qa.q: How many goals did Navneet score in the semi?
qa.a: Navneet scored twice in the semi.

qa.q: Why does Navneet believe the miss is personal but the goals are luck?
qa.a: Navneet has a habit of seeing setbacks as personal, permanent and everywhere while explaining successes away, and it feels like honesty rather than a habit.

qa.q: What choice does Thomas offer at the turning point, and why could it help?
qa.a: Five penalties on Friday: a small test that could give Navneet real evidence instead of the gloomy story.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Navneet's 'rule'?
qa.a: Thomas finds it strange that the goals don't count, and seems to see a teammate talking their way out of something they are good at.

grounding: A teenager treats one missed penalty as proof of failing at everything, dismisses successes as luck, and calls the pessimism honesty.

passage:
Monday. The contract law results went up: Disha, 34, fail. In the hostel corridor her inner voice was loud. You're not law material. Everyone knew it except you. She lay on her bed and skipped dinner.
Wednesday. Kalyani sat at the end of Disha's bed with the answer script. "Okay. What's the actual evidence?" Disha made herself look. Question 1, full marks. Question 2, good. Questions 4 and 5, blank. She had run out of time. "So... I do know the law," she said slowly. "I just spent forty minutes on question 3."
Saturday. No speeches about believing in herself. Just one change: she timed three past papers with the phone alarm, twenty-five minutes a question, and moved on when it rang. The inner voice still muttered. She checked it against the clock.

qa.q: What did Disha score in contract law?
qa.a: 34, a fail.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as the inner voice grew loud on Monday?
qa.a: She felt crushed and ashamed, believing she wasn't law material and everyone knew it except her, so she lay on the bed and skipped dinner.

qa.q: What one change did Disha pick, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: Timing past papers at twenty-five minutes a question, because the evidence showed the problem was running out of time, not knowing the law 👍

qa.q: How did Kalyani's question change the way Disha saw the result?
qa.a: Kalyani asked for the actual evidence instead of cheering Disha up, which let Disha find the real cause in the script herself.

grounding: A student who fails an exam checks the harsh story against the answer script, finds a different explanation, and makes one concrete change.

passage: Divyansh, you failed one exam and now you say you'll drop out. Sit. Your Lakshmi Paati failed too, you know. In 1978, second year of chemistry at the women's college, I got 28 in organic. That night I wrote in my notebook, "I am not clever enough for science." My roommate, a practical girl, took the notebook and said, "Now write the proof under it." So I did. Proof I'm not clever: I failed organic. Proof I am: I topped physical chemistry. Other reasons I failed: I skipped the reaction charts to rehearse for the dance show. Suddenly it wasn't a verdict, it was a list. I made one change, one chart every night, and passed the supplementary easily. I didn't feel cheerful, kanna. I just felt accurate.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi score in organic chemistry in 1978?
What did Lakshmi believe on the night of the result?
qa.a: Lakshmi believed "I am not clever enough for science", taking one failed paper as a verdict on everything.

qa.q: Why was the roommate's "Now write the proof under it" so useful?
qa.a: It turned the harsh belief into a list of evidence and other reasons, like the skipped reaction charts, which pointed to one change: a chart every night.

qa.q: How might Divyansh hear "I didn't feel cheerful, I just felt accurate"?
qa.a: Divyansh may feel relieved that nobody is demanding forced cheer, only an honest look at the facts behind one failed exam.

grounding: An elder recalls failing an exam, writing down the evidence for and against the harsh story, finding another explanation and making one change.

passage: Chandrika had been at the learning centre in Indore only a month, long enough to notice how differently her two seniors talked about the funding gap. The grant renewal was late, and forty girls were halfway through the coding course. "Relax, everything will be fine," Santosh said at every meeting, waving away the spreadsheet. "Donors always come through." He booked the fancy hall for graduation anyway. Rukhsar didn't promise it would be fine. She said, "I think we can keep the course running if we work for it." Then she listed three smaller donors to call, moved classes into the free community room, and asked the laptop vendor for a two-month delay. Chandrika helped her with the calls. When the grant arrived six weeks late, the course hadn't missed a day. Santosh said, "Told you." Chandrika thought of the lost hall deposit and said nothing.

qa.q: How many girls were halfway through the coding course?
qa.a: Forty girls.

qa.q: What might Chandrika have been thinking when Santosh said "Told you"?
qa.a: She was likely thinking of the lost hall deposit, and that the course survived because of Rukhsar's planning, not because everything was simply fine.

qa.q: Which approach to the funding gap worked, and why?
qa.a: Rukhsar's: she hoped the course could continue but backed that hope with donor calls, a free room and a delay from the vendor, so nothing rested on luck.

qa.q: How might Santosh see his own part in the story?
qa.a: Santosh probably believes his confidence was proven right, without noticing that others' planning covered the risks he waved away.

grounding: A new colleague watches one senior insist all will be fine while ignoring risk, and another hope and plan in ways that keep a course running.

passage:
"Anirban, the payment page crashes on older phones. Testing found it this morning."
"Sharmila, relax. It'll be fine. Launches always work out."
"Half our users have older phones."
"Positive thinking, yaar. Don't jinx it."
Across the table, Mallika looked up from her laptop.
"I think we can still launch Monday. Just not like this. If I fix the crash tonight, can you test it tomorrow, Sharmila?"
"Yes."
"And we keep the old payment page as a backup switch, just in case."
"You think it'll fail?" Anirban asked.
"I think it can work if we do the work."
Sharmila looked from one to the other, then opened her calendar and blocked out Saturday.
On Monday, the crash report stayed empty.

qa.q: What did testing find that morning?
qa.a: The payment page crashes on older phones.

qa.q: What does "Don't jinx it" suggest about how Anirban feels about the bug?
qa.a: It suggests Anirban wants to avoid thinking about the risk at all, treating worry as bad luck rather than as useful information.

qa.q: Which plan made Monday's empty crash report possible?
qa.a: Mallika's: fixing the crash that night, testing it on Saturday, and keeping the old payment page as a backup switch.

qa.q: How might Sharmila, watching both colleagues, describe the difference between them?
qa.a: Both were hopeful, but only Mallika tied the hope to fixes and a backup, which is why Sharmila blocked out Saturday to help.

grounding: A colleague watches one teammate wave away a known bug with 'it'll be fine' while another hopes and plans, and the planning makes the launch work.

passage:
"Rejected. Again. Mohit, I'm done. Two years of planning for that master's, gone."
"That's awful, Nitin. I'm so sorry."
"Don't tell me it happens for a reason."
"I won't. It's rubbish, and you're allowed to feel rubbish."
The balcony fan creaked through a long pause.
"I keep thinking I've wasted two years."
"Can I ask something? Out of all this, what's actually fixed?"
"The rejection. This intake is gone."
"Okay. And what isn't?"
"...The admission's still valid next year. They said I can defer. And the letter said my funding proof was unclear."
"So that part can change."
"Maybe. I could ask the bank for a clearer statement."
"Tomorrow?"
"Tomorrow. Just the email."
"I'll bring chai while you write it."

qa.q: What did the letter say about Nitin's funding proof?
qa.a: That it was unclear.

qa.q: What was Nitin afraid of when saying "Don't tell me it happens for a reason"?
qa.a: Nitin felt crushed and was afraid of being brushed off with empty comfort instead of being heard.

qa.q: How did Mohit help Nitin reach one small next step?
qa.a: Mohit first accepted the pain, then asked what was fixed and what wasn't, which led Nitin to the deferral and one email to the bank tomorrow.

qa.q: What would change if Mohit had opened with "Cheer up, it'll work out"?
qa.a: Nitin would likely have felt dismissed and shut down, never reaching the calmer question of what could still change.

grounding: A friend listens to despair after a rejection without dismissing it, then helps separate what is fixed from what can change and find one small step.

passage: I'm Rajni. Last winter my friend Nikita lost her first job at a physio clinic, cut with three others the same afternoon. She called me from the bus stop, crying so hard I could barely hear. "I'm useless. I'll never get another job." Everything in me wanted to say, "Of course you will!" I didn't. I went over with bread omelettes and listened for a whole hour while she said all the worst things. When she'd run out, I asked, "Which parts can't change, and which can?" She thought. The layoff couldn't. Her degree, her good patient reviews and the two clinics hiring near her could. We picked one small step: rewrite the CV that night. Just the CV. She got a callback in three weeks. I don't think I cheered her up. I think I gave her somewhere to put her feet.

qa.q: Where did Nikita call from?
qa.a: From the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Rajni want to say at first, and why hold back?
qa.a: Rajni wanted to say "Of course you will!", but sensed Nikita needed to be heard first rather than rushed into cheer.

qa.q: What small step did they choose, and why was it enough?
qa.a: Rewriting the CV that night, one clear thing within Nikita's control, which turned a huge fear into something doable.

qa.q: How might Nikita remember that evening?
qa.a: Nikita probably remembers being allowed to say the worst things without being corrected, then finding solid ground in what could still change 🤍

grounding: A friend listens fully to someone's despair after a job loss, then helps separate what is fixed from what can change and pick one small step.

passage: At the library's toddler morning in Lisbon, Priscila, two, dropped her biscuit and wailed. Freya, beside her with a shape sorter, froze. She stared at Priscila's red face. Her own lip wobbled, and then she was crying too, loud and hard, with no biscuit trouble at all. Across the rug, a baby boy stopped clapping and crawled fast to his papa. Freya's mum scooped up both girls and hummed. Slowly the sobs became hiccups.

qa.q: What did Priscila drop?
qa.a: Her biscuit.

qa.q: Why did Freya start crying when nothing had happened to her?
qa.a: She saw Priscila's red face and heard the wail, and the upset seemed to pass straight to her without her knowing why.

qa.q: How did Freya's mum help the crying settle?
qa.a: She scooped up both girls and hummed, giving them a calm, steady feeling to settle into.

qa.q: How might the baby boy across the rug have felt?
qa.a: He seemed worried by the crying, stopping his clapping and crawling fast to his papa for comfort.

grounding: One toddler's crying spreads to another who cries without knowing why, and a nearby baby looks worried.

passage: I'm Suraj, and I help at my aunt's daycare after college. Yesterday at nap time, little Aarush woke and cried for his mother. Preeti, one and a half, sat straight up on the next mat and stared at him. Her face crumpled. Then she was crying too, big tears, though nothing had happened to her. A toddler in the corner joined in. My aunt put on a slow lullaby and sat down among the mats, patting backs.

qa.q: What did Aarush cry for?
qa.a: For his mother.

qa.q: Why might Preeti have started crying though nothing had happened to her?
qa.a: Seeing Aarush upset right beside her seems to have made her feel upset too, the feeling spreading before she could know why.

qa.q: Why was the aunt's calm response a good choice?
qa.a: A slow lullaby and gentle patting gave the children a calm feeling to catch instead of more crying.

qa.q: What might nap time have looked like to Suraj, watching the crying spread?
qa.a: Suraj saw one child cry and others join in within moments, which likely felt puzzling and a little overwhelming.

grounding: A daycare helper watches one toddler's crying spread to others who cry without knowing why.
